name: LM Studio
license: Proprietary, free for personal and work use; the `lms` CLI, the lmstudio-js and lmstudio-python SDKs and the MLX engine are MIT
summary: A free, closed-source desktop app and headless daemon that downloads open-weight models from Hugging Face, runs them on your own machine with llama.cpp or Apple’s MLX, and serves them on OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible endpoints at localhost:1234.
intro: LM Studio searches Hugging Face for builds of open models, downloads the weights to disk and runs them with an LM Runtime: llama.cpp (GGUF files) on macOS, Windows and Linux, and Apple’s MLX on Apple Silicon. Runtimes update separately from the app. Once a model is on disk the app works offline: chats, attached documents and the local server stay on the machine, and only model search, downloads, runtime downloads and update checks reach the network. A document short enough to fit the model’s context is added whole; a longer one goes through built-in retrieval (RAG). It runs on Apple Silicon Macs with macOS 14 or newer, x64 and ARM Windows, and x64 and ARM64 Linux as an AppImage.

The Developer tab or `lms server start` opens an HTTP server on port 1234 with LM Studio’s own REST API, OpenAI-compatible endpoints (`/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/responses`, `/v1/embeddings`) and, since 0.4.1, an Anthropic-compatible `/v1/messages`, so existing SDKs, Codex and Claude Code reach local models by changing a base URL. A model loads just in time on its first request and unloads after an idle TTL, 60 minutes by default; with Auto-Evict on, at most one JIT-loaded model stays in memory. Version 0.4.0 (January 2026) split the core from the GUI as llmster, a daemon for Linux servers, GPU rigs without a display and CI, and added parallel requests with continuous batching to the llama.cpp engine.

The app itself is closed source but free, and since July 2025 that includes use at work without a separate commercial license. Element Labs sells an Enterprise plan with SSO and model and MCP gating. In July 2026 it also released LM Studio Bionic, a separate agent app that runs local models through the LM Studio runtime or larger open models on its billed LM Studio Secure Cloud.
strengths: Prompts, documents and weights stay on your machine once a model is downloaded, and the app works with no network connection
Two engines: llama.cpp on every platform and MLX on Apple Silicon, where Element Labs measured Llama 3.2 1B at about 250 tokens per second on an M3 Max when MLX support shipped
Drop-in local endpoints for OpenAI and Anthropic clients, with just-in-time loading, idle TTL and auto-evict so editors and agents can switch models without manual loading
Runs headless as llmster on Linux servers and in CI, driven by the same `lms` CLI as the desktop app
limits: The app is closed source; only the CLI, SDKs and MLX engine are open (MIT), so the core can’t be audited or forked

Model size and speed are bounded by your hardware: the docs recommend 16 GB of RAM and, on Windows, at least 4 GB of dedicated VRAM, and say 8 GB Macs should stick to small models and modest context sizes
No Intel Macs, x64 Windows PCs need AVX2, and the Linux build is not well tested on Ubuntu releases newer than 22
Continuous batching arrived in 0.4.0 for the llama.cpp engine only; Element Labs said the MLX engine would follow

snippet.title: Install the headless daemon, download a model and serve it on localhost:1234
source: curl -fsSL https://lmstudio.ai/install.sh | bash   # llmster; the desktop app ships lms too
lms load openai/gpt-oss-20b --ttl 3600             # unload after an idle hour

story: LM Studio launched in May 2023 as a desktop app for running open models on a personal computer. Its maker, Element Labs, describes the premise as AI that is accessible to people on their own machines, “with no reliance on an external party, and with complete privacy.” It stayed a small team: nine people in July 2025.

The app grew from a chat window into a local AI server. In May 2024 it gained `lms`, an MIT-licensed command-line tool developed on GitHub. In October 2024 version 0.3.4 added an MLX engine for Apple Silicon beside llama.cpp. In July 2025 Element Labs dropped the rule that work use needed a separate commercial license, after seeing teams avoid the app rather than start a procurement process. Version 0.4.0 in January 2026 separated the core from the GUI as the llmster daemon and added parallel requests, and 0.4.1 added an Anthropic-compatible endpoint so Claude Code could use local models.

In July 2026 Element Labs launched LM Studio Bionic, a separate agent app for coding and document work. It runs local models through the LM Studio runtime and larger open models on LM Studio Secure Cloud, which Element Labs says keeps no data after a request.

choices.choice: Run open models on the user’s own machine
choices.why: The team believes AI should be usable on your own computer without relying on an outside party, and with complete privacy.
MLX runs on-device models efficiently on Apple Silicon, and packaging engines as runtimes lets them update without a full app release.

choices.choice: Free at work, paid Enterprise features
choices.why: Requiring a commercial license for work use made adoption at companies high-friction, so Element Labs charges only for team needs such as SSO and model or MCP gating.

choices.choice: Split the core from the GUI
choices.why: To run the same model serving on Linux servers, GPU rigs without a screen, CI pipelines and Colab.
